intro: You've written persuasive texts with the rule of three, anaphora and antithesis, and your voice can already carry praise, doubt or warmth. Now you'll take it all onto a stage: a keynote-style talk built on **one big idea**, rhetoric that works for the ear (pauses, questions, contrasts, callbacks), and the skill of **reading the room** and adapting as you speak. Warm-up: think of a speech you still remember. What was its one big idea?
teachingNotes: Speaking lesson (strand SP). Recap the chain in one line each, don't re-teach: c1-presentations-advanced (a hook instead of a name-and-topic opening, a four-part story with concrete detail, keyword notes instead of a script, calm Q&A), c2-rhetoric (devices on the page: tricolon / rule of three, anaphora, parallelism, climax, antithesis, chiasmus, rhetorical questions, ethos/pathos/logos, a call to action) and c2-pron-natural (attitude in the voice; adapting pace, volume, pausing and articulation to the room and the audience). New here: the shape of a keynote-style talk, rhetoric for the EAR (timing, pauses, repetition, callbacks), delivery that carries it (eye contact, movement, voice variety), and reading the room = adapting live to the audience's signals. Contexts (fictional, never real event names): a keynote at a startup summit in Jakarta, a graduation speech at a university in Yogyakarta, a TEDx-style talk in Bandung; Sari, Budi, Dimas, Rina, Pak Hasan, Dr. Wulan, Bu Ratna. All stories and figures are practice examples.

Objective keynote-talk. A keynote (pidato utama) is built on ONE big idea, a sentence the audience can repeat on the way home (Build for the person with the cheapest phone.); anything that doesn't serve it is cut. A shape for 15–20 minutes (about 130 words a minute, so 18 minutes ≈ 2,300 words): hook (about 1 minute) → the big idea in one sentence and why it matters to them → three parts of 4–5 minutes, each a point + a story or evidence + a link back to the idea → a close (1–2 minutes) that calls back to the opening story or image, shows what has changed and ends on the idea, then a simple 'Thank you.' Listeners can't re-read, so: preview the map, signpost every turn (That's the first wall. Now, the second: words.), recap, and repeat the key line word for word two or three times. Write for the ear: short sentences (one idea each), concrete words (forty orders in one morning, not a significant increase in transaction volume; use, not utilise), active voice (Our drivers delivered 3,000 parcels), you/we and questions to the audience. Protocol: the long Indonesian greeting (Yang terhormat Bapak Rektor, yang kami hormati …, yang berbahagia …; puji syukur …) becomes one line in English (Rector, distinguished guests, graduates and families: good morning. / Good morning, everyone.), then straight to the hook; the close is the callback, not 'Sekian dan terima kasih' → 'That's all. Thank you.'

Objective spoken-rhetoric. Spoken, timing does half the work. Notation (prompts, notes, artifact only): CAPITALS = stressed word, | = short pause, || = long pause, ↘ fall. Rule of three: three short items of the same shape, a short pause before the third and a fall ↘ on it. Anaphora aloud: the same opening said the same way each time, stress on what changes. Rhetorical question: ask, then stop for 2–3 seconds; answering at once, or firing a second question, kills it. A rhetorical question expects no spoken answer; a show-of-hands question (Hands up if …) is a real question, used to re-engage a room. Power pause: a pause BEFORE the key word or line (…was || trust). Contrast pair (spoken antithesis): stress both opposites (not SMARTER phones, SIMPLER apps). Callback: an image, word or line from the opening that returns later, above all at the close. Delivery: eye contact with one person for a whole sentence, then someone in another part of the room; movement with purpose (walk on a transition, stand still for the key line; no constant pacing); voice variety (pace, volume, pitch). Devices at key moments only: one rhetorical question per part, one big contrast, one callback. Devices often combine (an anaphora can also be a tricolon): accept any correct label and name the others present.

Objective read-the-room (membaca suasana): watch the audience and adapt; a keynote is a plan, not a script to finish word for word. Sign → adaptation: puzzled faces or whispering → say it again in plain words with a quick example (Let me put that another way. / In other words, …); blank looks at a technical term → skip the jargon or explain it in one line; phones out, restlessness, shifting in seats (often in a long data section) → cut the section short, jump to the next story, or ask a quick show-of-hands question; people at the back leaning forward or cupping their ears → speak louder, move closer to the microphone, speak to the back row; frowning while writing, 'Could you repeat that number?' → slow down, repeat it, show it; laughter, nodding, photos of a slide → it's working, let it land; silence after 'Any questions?' → often shyness or waiting for someone to go first (sungkan, malu), not hostility: give them a moment, offer a question you often get, or a 30-second chat with a neighbour; running late → never speed up and never run over the next speaker's time: cut calmly, In the interest of time, I'll skip … (In the interests of time is also common, especially in British English: accept both); a joke falls flat → don't explain it, don't apologise again and again; smile, one light line or none, move on. Plan adaptations in advance: one section to cut, one extra example, one show-of-hands question.

The node lists no commonErrors; watch for these: one talk with five or seven ideas and no single message; a long protocol greeting that eats the hook; ending with 'That's all. Thank you.' or new material at the end instead of a callback; a written naskah pidato read aloud, full of long sentences, nominalisations and passives (telah dilaksanakan → has been carried out; dapat disimpulkan bahwa → it can be concluded that); the key line said once and never again; answering your own rhetorical question at once; pausing in the middle of a phrase instead of before the key word; eyes on the slides, the notes or the ceiling; constant pacing; one speed for 18 minutes; speeding up when running late; explaining or repeatedly apologising for a flat joke; wordplay (plesetan) that doesn't survive translation; reading silence after a question as rejection.

Audio and C2 honesty. Every recording is one plain TTS voice reading plain text: it cannot make a chosen pause, stress or tone, so spoken English fields (tiles, examples, listen) are plain spelling and the notation lives in notes, prompts, options and the artifact. Listening questions test only what is in the WORDS (which device a line uses). Much of public speaking is style and judgement: accept any reasonable structure, device or adaptation, and test only clear cases (a callback close vs 'That's all'; a pause after a rhetorical question vs answering at once; plain words vs repeating jargon louder; cutting vs speeding up). Don't quote real speeches or name real events; famous speakers and TED may be named as places to watch. Don't teach slide design, stage fright therapy, or speech-writing for others. When the learner drafts a talk, give feedback in this order: is the one big idea clear? does the close call back to the opening? are the sentences written for the ear? one device used well (or overused)? then ONE concrete improvement.

keyPoints.title: One big idea, a clear shape, built for the ear
keyPoints.explanation: Build the talk on one big idea: one sentence the audience can repeat at home. For 15–20 minutes: a hook, the idea in one sentence, three parts (each a point plus a story or evidence), and a close that calls back to the opening. Listeners can't re-read, so preview, signpost, recap and repeat your key line. Write for the ear: short sentences, concrete words, active voice. Keep the protocol greeting to one line.

examples.en: Here's my one idea for today: build for the person with the cheapest phone.
examples.id: Ini satu gagasan saya hari ini: buatlah untuk orang dengan ponsel termurah.

examples.en: That's the first wall. Now, the second: words.
examples.id: Itu tembok pertama. Sekarang, yang kedua: kata-kata.

examples.en: Remember Bu Ratna? Last month she took forty orders in one morning.
examples.id: Ingat Bu Ratna? Bulan lalu dia menerima empat puluh pesanan dalam satu pagi.

id.title: Satu gagasan besar, bentuk yang jelas, ditulis untuk didengar
id.explanation: Bangun pidatomu di atas satu gagasan besar: satu kalimat yang bisa diulang audiens sesampainya di rumah. Untuk 15–20 menit: pengait (hook), gagasan itu dalam satu kalimat, tiga bagian (masing-masing satu poin plus cerita atau bukti), dan penutup yang kembali ke pembukaan (callback). Pendengar tidak bisa membaca ulang, jadi beri gambaran awal, penanda arah, rangkuman, dan ulangi kalimat kuncimu. Tulis untuk didengar: kalimat pendek, kata yang konkret, kalimat aktif. Salam protokoler cukup satu baris.

keyPoints.title: Rhetoric for the ear: timing does half the work
keyPoints.explanation: Rule of three: three short, same-shape items, a pause before the third and a fall on it. Anaphora: the same opening each time, stress on what changes. Rhetorical question: ask, then stop for two or three seconds. Power pause: a pause before the key word. Contrast pair: stress both opposites. Callback: an image from the opening comes back. Carry them with eye contact, movement with purpose and voice variety, and use them at key moments only.

examples.en: Who here has ever waited three days for a parcel that never came?
examples.id: Siapa di sini yang pernah menunggu tiga hari untuk paket yang tidak pernah datang? (pertanyaan retoris: lalu diam || 2–3 detik)

examples.en: And the one thing that changed everything was trust.
examples.id: Dan satu hal yang mengubah segalanya adalah kepercayaan. (jeda kuat: …was || TRUST)

examples.en: We don't need smarter phones. We need simpler apps.
examples.id: Kita tidak butuh ponsel yang lebih pintar. Kita butuh aplikasi yang lebih sederhana. (pasangan kontras: tekan SMARTER dan SIMPLER)

id.title: Retorika untuk telinga: waktu yang tepat melakukan separuh pekerjaan
id.explanation: Rule of three: tiga bagian pendek berbentuk sama, jeda sebelum yang ketiga dan nada turun di situ. Anafora: pembuka yang sama setiap kali, tekanan pada bagian yang berubah. Pertanyaan retoris: tanyakan, lalu diam dua atau tiga detik. Power pause: jeda sebelum kata kunci. Pasangan kontras: tekan kedua kata yang berlawanan. Callback: gambaran dari pembukaan muncul lagi. Bawakan semuanya dengan kontak mata, gerakan yang punya tujuan dan variasi suara, dan pakai hanya di saat-saat penting.

keyPoints.title: Read the room and adapt
keyPoints.explanation: Watch the audience while you speak. Puzzled faces: say it again in plain words with an example. Phones out or restless: cut the section short, go to a story or ask a quick show of hands. Leaning forward at the back: speak louder. 'Could you repeat that?': slow down. Silence after 'Any questions?' is often shyness: give them a moment. Running late: cut calmly ('In the interest of time, …'), never speed up. A joke falls flat: don't explain it or keep apologising; smile and move on.

examples.en: Let me put that another way.
examples.id: Saya jelaskan dengan cara lain. (setelah melihat wajah-wajah bingung)

examples.en: Hands up if you've ever sent a message to the wrong group.
examples.id: Angkat tangan kalau kamu pernah mengirim pesan ke grup yang salah. (membangunkan ruangan yang mulai gelisah)

examples.en: In the interest of time, I'll go straight to the last story.
examples.id: Mengingat waktu, saya langsung ke cerita terakhir. (waktu hampir habis)

id.title: Baca suasana dan sesuaikan diri
id.explanation: Perhatikan audiens selagi kamu bicara. Wajah bingung: ulangi dengan kata-kata sederhana dan satu contoh. Ponsel mulai keluar atau audiens gelisah: persingkat bagian itu, pindah ke cerita, atau minta audiens angkat tangan. Orang di belakang mencondongkan badan ke depan: bicara lebih keras. 'Could you repeat that?': pelankan tempo. Hening setelah 'Any questions?' sering hanya karena sungkan: beri mereka waktu sebentar. Waktu hampir habis: potong dengan tenang ('In the interest of time, …'), jangan malah bicara lebih cepat. Lelucon tidak lucu: jangan dijelaskan dan jangan minta maaf berkali-kali; tersenyum lalu lanjutkan.

guidedPractice.prompt: Sari ends the first part of her keynote at a startup summit in Jakarta and wants to remind the audience where they are. Complete the recap signpost with ONE word: 'So, ___ recap: a weak signal is the first wall between Bu Ratna and her customers.'
guidedPractice.hint: A fixed phrase used to start a short summary: '___ sum up', '___ recap'.

guidedPractice.prompt: Writing for the ear: which word is easier for a listener, 'utilise' or 'use'? Write it.
guidedPractice.hint: Short, everyday words are easier to catch when you can't re-read.

guidedPractice.prompt: At a TEDx-style talk in Bandung, Rina asks: 'Is this really the city we want to leave our children?' Then she says nothing for three seconds. What kind of question is it? Write two words.
guidedPractice.hint: Nobody is expected to answer aloud: the answer is obvious.

guidedPractice.prompt: Budi's audience is getting restless during his data section, so he asks a quick question to wake them up. Complete with ONE word: 'Hands ___ if you've ever waited more than a week for a parcel.'
guidedPractice.hint: What do people do with their hands to answer 'yes' in a big room?

independentPractice.prompt: Dimas has 18 minutes for a TEDx-style talk in Bandung. In the keynote shape from this lesson, how many main parts sit between the big idea and the close? Write a number.
independentPractice.hint: Enough to feel complete, few enough to remember.

independentPractice.prompt: Pak Hasan says: 'And the one thing that saved the company was ... our drivers.' He stops for two seconds just before 'our drivers'. What do we call a pause placed right before the key words? Write two words.
independentPractice.hint: It comes right before the key words and makes everyone wait for them.

independentPractice.prompt: During Dr. Wulan's talk, many faces look puzzled after a technical term. Complete her next line with ONE word: 'Let me put that another ___.'

assessment.prompt: In a practice TEDx-style talk in Bandung, Rina says: 'This city taught me to work hard. This city taught me to share. This city taught me never to give up.' Which device is it? Choose from: antithesis, anaphora, rhetorical question, callback. Write the name.
assessment.rubric: Correct: anaphora (the same words, 'This city taught me', open three sentences in a row; said aloud, the repeated words give the ear a beat and the stress falls on what changes). 'tricolon' or 'rule of three' = 70 (true, it has three parts, but it isn't in the list and the repeated opening is the device asked about). 'parallelism' = 50. 'antithesis' = 0 (no opposite ideas). 'rhetorical question' = 0 (there's no question). 'callback' = 0 (nothing returns from an opening).

assessment.prompt: Sari opens her practice keynote at a startup summit in Jakarta with a story: her first phone had a cracked screen, and she built her first app on it. Fifteen minutes later she ends: 'That cracked phone is still on my desk. Every morning, it reminds me who we build for.' What do we call a close that returns to the opening story? Choose from: hook, callback, signpost, preview. Write one word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: callback (the cracked phone from the opening comes back at the end, now carrying the big idea: build for people like her). 'bookend' or 'bookending' = 80 (a real term for the same idea, but not in the list). 'hook' = 10 (the cracked-phone story was the hook at the start; the close that returns to it is the callback). 'signpost' or 'preview' = 0 (those guide listeners through the middle of a talk).

assessment.prompt: Dimas is giving a practice graduation speech at a university in Yogyakarta. He asks the hall a rhetorical question: 'What would you do with one extra hour every day?' What should he do right after it? Choose from: answer it at once, pause, ask another question. Write your choice.
acceptableAnswers: pause for two or three seconds
assessment.rubric: Correct: pause (two or three seconds of silence, so everyone answers the question in their own head; that moment is why the question works). Any wording that means a short silence = 100. 'answer it at once' = 0 (it takes the moment away before the audience can think). 'ask another question' = 0 (questions fired in a row sound like a lecture and leave no time to think).

assessment.prompt: Pak Hasan is speaking without a microphone in a long hall in Surabaya. He notices people in the back rows leaning forward, and one man cups his hand behind his ear. Which adaptation fits best? Choose from: speak louder, cut a section, tell a joke, skip the jargon. Write your choice.
assessment.rubric: Correct: speak louder (leaning forward and a hand cupped behind the ear mean the back rows can't hear; he should project his voice to the back row, and could also ask 'Can everyone at the back hear me?'). Any wording meaning louder or projecting the voice = 100. 'speak more slowly' = 40 (it may help a little, but the sign is about volume). 'cut a section', 'tell a joke' or 'skip the jargon' = 0 (none of them fixes a sound problem).

assessment.prompt: Rina's talk at a conference in Jakarta is running five minutes late, and the next speaker is waiting. She wants to drop her last case study calmly. Complete with ONE word: 'In the ___ of time, I'll skip the last case study and go straight to my conclusion.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: interest (In the interest of time = because time is short; In the interests of time is also common, especially in British English = 100). 'sake' = 30 (for the sake of time is heard, but it isn't this fixed phrase and doesn't fit 'In the ___ of'). 'name', 'middle' or any other word = 0.

assessment.prompt: Budi is nervous and races through the figures in his keynote at a startup summit in Jakarta. Several people frown as they try to write the numbers down, and one asks, 'Sorry, could you repeat that last number?' Which adaptation fits best? Choose from: speed up, slow down, add a joke, skip the questions. Write your choice.
acceptableAnswers: slow down and repeat the number
assessment.rubric: Correct: slow down (the audience can't follow the numbers; he should repeat the number, say key figures slowly with a short pause before them, and show them on a slide). Any wording meaning a slower pace = 100. 'speed up' = 0 (the nervous habit that caused the problem). 'add a joke' = 0. 'skip the questions' = 0 (the question is the useful signal).

assessment.prompt: Dr. Wulan's draft for a practice keynote in Bandung says: 'Mistakes were made by our team.' Writing for the ear, she changes it to the active voice, so listeners hear who did what. Complete with ONE word: 'Our team ___ mistakes.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: made (active voice: the doer, our team, comes first, then the action: Our team made mistakes. It's shorter, clearer to hear, and honest about who was responsible). 'make' = 40 (active, but the tense changes from past to present). 'has made' or 'have made' = 60 (two words, but active and correct). 'were made' or 'was made' = 0 (still passive).

material.title: One big idea, one clear shape

blocks.text:
**Quick recap:** you already have the parts. From *Persuasive Presentations* (C1): a hook, a four-part story with a point, keyword notes. From *Rhetoric & Persuasion*: devices on the page (tricolon, anaphora, antithesis). From *Natural Prosody & Nuance*: a voice that carries attitude and fits the room. Now we put them together on a stage.

A **keynote** (*pidato utama*) is the big talk that opens or anchors an event: a startup summit, a graduation, a TEDx-style evening. Its secret is **one big idea** (*satu gagasan besar*): one sentence the audience can repeat on the way home. *Build for the person with the cheapest phone.* Everything in the talk serves that sentence. Anything that doesn't, you cut, however interesting it is.

**A shape for 15–20 minutes** (at about 130 words a minute, 18 minutes is roughly 2,300 words):
- **Hook** (about 1 minute): a short story, a surprising number or a question.
- **The big idea** (under a minute): say it in one sentence, and say why it matters to *them*.
- **Three parts** (4–5 minutes each): each one = a point + a story or piece of evidence + a link back to the big idea.
- **The close** (1–2 minutes): a **callback** (*kembali ke pembukaan*): return to the opening story or image, show what has changed, and end on the big idea. Then a simple *Thank you.*

Why three parts? Three feels complete and is easy to remember. Why a callback? It closes the circle: the audience feels the talk was planned from the first word, and the opening image now carries the whole idea. A close that adds **new** material (one more statistic, one more story) does the opposite: it opens a door just as you leave.

id.text:
**Kilas balik singkat:** bagian-bagiannya sudah kamu punya. Dari *Persuasive Presentations* (C1): pengait (hook), cerita empat bagian yang punya pesan, catatan kata kunci. Dari *Rhetoric & Persuasion*: gaya bahasa retoris di atas kertas (tricolon, anafora, antitesis). Dari *Natural Prosody & Nuance*: suara yang membawa sikap dan cocok dengan ruangan. Sekarang semuanya kita satukan di atas panggung.

**Keynote** (*pidato utama*) adalah pidato besar yang membuka atau menjadi pusat sebuah acara: startup summit, wisuda, malam bergaya TEDx. Rahasianya adalah **satu gagasan besar**: satu kalimat yang bisa diulang audiens dalam perjalanan pulang. *Build for the person with the cheapest phone.* Semua isi pidato melayani kalimat itu. Yang tidak melayaninya kamu buang, semenarik apa pun.

**Bentuk untuk 15–20 menit** (sekitar 130 kata per menit, jadi 18 menit kira-kira 2.300 kata):
- **Hook** (sekitar 1 menit): cerita singkat, angka yang mengejutkan, atau pertanyaan.
- **Gagasan besar** (kurang dari semenit): ucapkan dalam satu kalimat, dan katakan mengapa itu penting bagi *mereka*.
- **Tiga bagian** (masing-masing 4–5 menit): tiap bagian = satu poin + satu cerita atau bukti + kaitan kembali ke gagasan besar.
- **Penutup** (1–2 menit): **callback** (*kembali ke pembukaan*): kembali ke cerita atau gambaran pembuka, tunjukkan apa yang sudah berubah, dan akhiri dengan gagasan besar. Lalu cukup *Thank you.*

Kenapa tiga bagian? Tiga terasa lengkap dan mudah diingat. Kenapa callback? Callback menutup lingkaran: audiens merasa pidatonya sudah direncanakan sejak kata pertama, dan gambaran pembuka itu sekarang membawa seluruh gagasan. Penutup yang menambah materi **baru** (satu statistik lagi, satu cerita lagi) justru sebaliknya: seperti membuka pintu baru tepat saat kamu pamit.

rows.en: Last March, Bu Ratna lost three orders in one morning because no driver could find her stall.
rows.id: Maret lalu, Bu Ratna kehilangan tiga pesanan dalam satu pagi karena tidak ada pengemudi yang bisa menemukan lapaknya.
rows.note: hook: a short story with a name, a place and a number

id.note: hook: cerita singkat dengan nama, tempat dan angka

rows.en: Here's my one idea for today: build for the person with the cheapest phone.
rows.id: Ini satu gagasan saya hari ini: buatlah untuk orang dengan ponsel termurah.
rows.note: the big idea in one sentence
part one opens with a clear point

id.note: bagian pertama dibuka dengan poin yang jelas

rows.en: Remember Bu Ratna? Last month she took forty orders in one morning, on the same cheap phone.
rows.id: Ingat Bu Ratna? Bulan lalu dia menerima empat puluh pesanan dalam satu pagi, dengan ponsel murah yang sama.
rows.note: the close: a callback to the hook, now changed

id.note: penutup: callback ke hook, yang sekarang sudah berubah

blocks.text: **The protocol greeting.** A formal Indonesian speech often opens with a long list: *Yang terhormat Bapak Rektor, yang kami hormati para dekan, yang berbahagia para wisudawan …*, then *puji syukur …*. In English, keep it to one line and go straight to your hook: *Rector, distinguished guests, graduates and families: good morning.* At a startup summit or a TEDx-style talk, *Good morning, everyone* is enough. Every minute of protocol is a minute taken from your hook. Close the same way: not *Sekian dan terima kasih* → *That's all. Thank you.*, but your callback, then a simple *Thank you.*

id.text: **Salam protokoler.** Pidato resmi berbahasa Indonesia sering dibuka dengan daftar panjang: *Yang terhormat Bapak Rektor, yang kami hormati para dekan, yang berbahagia para wisudawan …*, lalu *puji syukur …*. Dalam bahasa Inggris, cukup satu baris lalu langsung ke hook: *Rector, distinguished guests, graduates and families: good morning.* Di startup summit atau pidato bergaya TEDx, *Good morning, everyone* sudah cukup. Setiap menit untuk protokol adalah satu menit yang diambil dari hook-mu. Tutup dengan cara yang sama: bukan *Sekian dan terima kasih* → *That's all. Thank you.*, melainkan callback-mu, lalu cukup *Thank you.*

blocks.prompt: Rina has 18 minutes at a startup summit in Jakarta. Her draft has seven separate ideas, each with its own slide. What should she do first?
options: Speak faster so that all seven ideas fit.
Choose the one idea the others support, and cut what doesn't serve it.
Keep all seven and add a summary slide at the end.
blocks.explain: A keynote is built on **one big idea**. Seven ideas in 18 minutes means the audience remembers none. Speaking faster makes it worse, and a summary slide can't fix a talk with no single message.

id.prompt: Rina punya 18 menit di sebuah startup summit di Jakarta. Drafnya berisi tujuh gagasan terpisah, masing-masing dengan slide sendiri. Apa yang sebaiknya dia lakukan lebih dulu?
id.explain: Keynote dibangun di atas **satu gagasan besar**. Tujuh gagasan dalam 18 menit berarti audiens tidak akan ingat satu pun. Bicara lebih cepat malah memperburuknya, dan slide rangkuman tidak bisa menolong pidato yang tidak punya satu pesan utama.
options: Bicara lebih cepat agar tujuh gagasan muat.
Pilih satu gagasan yang didukung gagasan lain, lalu hapus yang tidak mendukungnya.
Pertahankan ketujuhnya dan tambahkan slide rangkuman di akhir.

id.title: Satu gagasan besar, satu bentuk yang jelas

material.title: Signposts and writing for the ear

blocks.text:
A reader can go back and re-read a sentence. A listener **can't**. So a talk needs things a text doesn't:
- **Preview** (*gambaran awal*): give them the map. *I'll tell you three stories: about a signal, a word and a handshake.*
- **Signposts** (*penanda arah*) between parts: *That's the first wall. Now, the second: words.*
- **Recap** (*rangkuman*): *So: a weak signal, a strange word, no trust. Three walls between Bu Ratna and her customers.*
- **Repeat the key line** word for word, two or three times: at the start, after a part, at the end. On the page that would be boring; in a hall, it's how the idea survives the moment someone looked at their phone.

**Write for the ear** (*menulis untuk didengar*):
- **Short sentences**: one idea per sentence. A listener can't hold a 40-word sentence with three clauses in their head.
- **Concrete words** (*kata yang konkret*, bisa dibayangkan): *forty orders in one morning*, not *a significant increase in transaction volume*; *use*, not *utilise*.
- **Active voice** (*kalimat aktif*): *Our drivers delivered 3,000 parcels*, not *3,000 parcels were delivered by our drivers*. The listener hears who did what, in that order.
- **Talk to them**: *you*, *we*, and questions: *Why does this matter to you?*

⚠ **The Indonesian trap:** a *naskah pidato* is usually written to be read, with long sentences, nouns made from verbs and many passives (*telah dilaksanakan*, *dapat disimpulkan bahwa*). Translated word by word, it becomes *It can be concluded that the implementation has been carried out*: correct, but heavy to hear. Say *We did it, and it worked.*

id.text:
Pembaca bisa kembali dan membaca ulang sebuah kalimat. Pendengar **tidak bisa**. Jadi pidato butuh hal-hal yang tidak dibutuhkan tulisan:
- **Preview** (*gambaran awal*): beri mereka peta. *I'll tell you three stories: about a signal, a word and a handshake.*
- **Signpost** (*penanda arah*) di antara bagian: *That's the first wall. Now, the second: words.*
- **Recap** (*rangkuman*): *So: a weak signal, a strange word, no trust. Three walls between Bu Ratna and her customers.*
- **Ulangi kalimat kunci** kata per kata, dua atau tiga kali: di awal, setelah satu bagian, di akhir. Di atas kertas itu membosankan; di aula, begitulah gagasanmu tetap hidup saat seseorang sempat melirik ponselnya.

**Menulis untuk didengar**:
- **Kalimat pendek**: satu gagasan per kalimat. Pendengar tidak sanggup menampung kalimat 40 kata dengan tiga anak kalimat.
- **Kata yang konkret** (bisa dibayangkan): *forty orders in one morning*, bukan *a significant increase in transaction volume*; *use*, bukan *utilise*.
- **Kalimat aktif**: *Our drivers delivered 3,000 parcels*, bukan *3,000 parcels were delivered by our drivers*. Pendengar mendengar siapa melakukan apa, dengan urutan itu.
- **Ajak bicara audiens**: *you*, *we*, dan pertanyaan: *Why does this matter to you?*

⚠ **Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** *naskah pidato* biasanya ditulis untuk dibaca, dengan kalimat panjang, kata benda yang dibentuk dari kata kerja, dan banyak kalimat pasif (*telah dilaksanakan*, *dapat disimpulkan bahwa*). Kalau diterjemahkan kata per kata, jadinya *It can be concluded that the implementation has been carried out*: benar, tapi berat didengar. Katakan saja *We did it, and it worked.*

rows.id: Ada tiga hal yang menghalangi: sinyal, kata-kata dan kepercayaan.

blocks.text: **Test your script with your mouth, not your eyes.** Read each paragraph aloud. If you run out of breath, the sentence is too long. If you stumble, the words are too written. Then cut the script down to keyword notes (from C1) and mark | where you'll pause and the word you'll stress.

id.text: **Uji naskahmu dengan mulut, bukan dengan mata.** Bacakan tiap paragraf dengan suara keras. Kalau napasmu habis, kalimatnya terlalu panjang. Kalau kamu tersandung, kata-katanya terlalu 'tulisan'. Lalu ringkas naskahnya menjadi catatan kata kunci (dari C1) dan beri tanda | di tempat kamu akan berhenti sejenak, serta kata yang akan kamu tekan.

blocks.prompt: Which sentence is written for the ear?
options: A significant reduction in delivery times was achieved following the implementation of the new system.
Delivery times, which had previously been a source of considerable concern among stakeholders, improved.
With the new system, our deliveries take two days, not five.
blocks.explain: It's short, concrete (two days, not five) and active: the listener hears it once and keeps it. The first sentence is passive and abstract (*a significant reduction … was achieved*); the second hides the point inside a long clause.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang ditulis untuk didengar?
id.explain: Kalimatnya pendek, konkret (dua hari, bukan lima) dan aktif: pendengar cukup mendengarnya sekali dan langsung ingat. Kalimat pertama pasif dan abstrak (*a significant reduction … was achieved*); kalimat kedua menyembunyikan pesannya di dalam anak kalimat yang panjang.

id.title: Penanda arah dan menulis untuk didengar

material.title: Rhetoric for the ear: pauses, questions, contrasts

blocks.text:
You met these devices on the page in *Rhetoric & Persuasion*. Spoken, they work differently, because **timing** now does half the work. Notation in this lesson: **CAPITALS** = stressed word, **|** = short pause, **||** = long pause, **↘** = the voice falls. (The app's recordings are one plain voice reading plain text, so they can't make these pauses or stresses: the marks are in the notes, and you say them aloud.)
- **The rule of three, spoken:** keep the three items short and the same shape, pause briefly before the third and let the voice fall on it: *slow, | expensive | and DANgerous ↘*.
- **Anaphora aloud** (*anafora*, the same words opening several sentences): the repeated words give the ear a beat to follow. Say them the same way each time, and stress what changes.
- **Rhetorical question + pause:** ask it, then **stop** for two or three seconds. The audience answers in their heads; that silence is the point. Answer too fast and you take the moment away.
- **The power pause** (*jeda kuat*): a pause **before** the key word or line: *And the one thing that changed everything was || trust.* The silence says 'listen now'.
- **Contrast pairs** (spoken antithesis, *pasangan kontras*): stress the two words that contrast: *We don't need SMARTER phones. | We need SIMPLER apps.*
- **Callback:** an image, word or line from the opening that comes back later, above all at the end. The audience recognises it, and recognising feels good.

**Delivery** (*cara membawakan*) carries the devices:
- **Eye contact** (*kontak mata*): look at one person for a whole sentence, then at someone in another part of the room (left, centre, the back), not at your slides or the ceiling.
- **Movement with purpose:** walk on a transition (a new part, a new spot on the stage) and **stand still** for the key line. Constant pacing looks nervous.
- **Voice variety:** change pace, volume and pitch (from *Natural Prosody & Nuance*): slower and lower for the serious moment, a little faster for the action in a story. One speed for 18 minutes puts people to sleep.

⚠ **Key moments only.** One rhetorical question per part, one big contrast, one callback. A device in every sentence sounds like an advertisement.

id.text:
Gaya bahasa ini sudah kamu temui di atas kertas di *Rhetoric & Persuasion*. Saat diucapkan, cara kerjanya berbeda, karena sekarang **waktu yang tepat** melakukan separuh pekerjaan. Notasi di pelajaran ini: **HURUF BESAR** = kata yang ditekan, **|** = jeda pendek, **||** = jeda panjang, **↘** = nada turun. (Rekaman di aplikasi adalah satu suara biasa yang membaca teks polos, jadi tidak bisa membuat jeda atau tekanan ini: tandanya ada di catatan, dan kamu yang mengucapkannya.)
- **Rule of three secara lisan:** buat ketiga bagiannya pendek dan berbentuk sama, berhenti sebentar sebelum yang ketiga dan biarkan nada turun di situ: *slow, | expensive | and DANgerous ↘*.
- **Anafora diucapkan** (kata yang sama membuka beberapa kalimat): kata yang berulang memberi telinga irama untuk diikuti. Ucapkan dengan cara yang sama setiap kali, dan tekan bagian yang berubah.
- **Pertanyaan retoris + jeda:** ajukan, lalu **diam** dua atau tiga detik. Audiens menjawab dalam hati; keheningan itulah intinya. Kalau kamu langsung menjawab, momen itu hilang.
- **Power pause** (*jeda kuat*): jeda **sebelum** kata atau kalimat kunci: *And the one thing that changed everything was || trust.* Keheningan itu berkata 'dengarkan sekarang'.
- **Pasangan kontras** (antitesis yang diucapkan): tekan dua kata yang berlawanan: *We don't need SMARTER phones. | We need SIMPLER apps.*
- **Callback:** gambaran, kata atau kalimat dari pembukaan yang muncul lagi, terutama di akhir. Audiens mengenalinya, dan mengenali sesuatu itu terasa menyenangkan.

**Cara membawakan** yang mendukung gaya bahasa itu:
- **Kontak mata:** tatap satu orang selama satu kalimat penuh, lalu orang lain di bagian ruangan yang berbeda (kiri, tengah, belakang), bukan slide atau langit-langit.
- **Bergerak dengan tujuan:** berjalanlah saat pindah bagian (bagian baru, posisi baru di panggung) dan **berdiri diam** saat kalimat kunci. Mondar-mandir terus terlihat gugup.
- **Variasi suara:** ubah tempo, volume dan tinggi nada (dari *Natural Prosody & Nuance*): lebih pelan dan lebih rendah untuk momen serius, sedikit lebih cepat untuk bagian aksi dalam cerita. Satu kecepatan selama 18 menit membuat orang mengantuk.

⚠ **Hanya di saat-saat penting.** Satu pertanyaan retoris per bagian, satu kontras besar, satu callback. Gaya bahasa di setiap kalimat terdengar seperti iklan.

blocks.prompt: Which version puts the power pause in the right place?
options: The || secret of our growth was not money. It was our drivers.
The secret of our || growth was not money. It was our drivers.
The secret of our growth was not money. It was || our drivers.
blocks.explain: The power pause goes right **before the key words**, *our drivers*: the silence makes everyone wait for the answer. A pause after *The* or in the middle of *our growth* breaks a phrase and sounds like you've lost your place.

id.prompt: Versi mana yang menaruh power pause di tempat yang tepat?
id.explain: Power pause diletakkan tepat **sebelum kata kunci**, *our drivers*: keheningan itu membuat semua orang menunggu jawabannya. Jeda setelah *The* atau di tengah *our growth* memotong satu frasa dan terdengar seolah kamu lupa sampai di mana.

id.title: Retorika untuk telinga: jeda, pertanyaan, kontras

blocks.text:
**Reading the room** (*membaca suasana*) means watching the audience while you speak, and changing your talk when they send a signal. A keynote is a plan, not a script you must finish word for word.

**Signs and what to do:**
- **Puzzled faces, people whispering to a neighbour** → they've lost you. Say it again in plain words with a quick example: *Let me put that another way.* / *In other words, …*
- **Blank looks at a technical term** → skip the jargon (*istilah teknis*) or explain it in one line.
- **Phones out, restlessness** (*gelisah*), **people shifting in their seats** → attention is dropping, often in a long data section. Cut the section short, jump to the next story, or ask a quick **show-of-hands question** (*minta audiens angkat tangan*): *Hands up if you've ever …*
- **People at the back leaning forward or cupping a hand behind an ear** → they can't hear. Speak louder, move closer to the microphone, speak to the back row.
- **Frowning while writing, 'Sorry, could you repeat that?'** → you're too fast, often on numbers. Slow down, repeat the number, show it on a slide.
- **Laughter, nodding, people photographing a slide** → it's working. Don't rush past it: let the laugh finish, give the slide a moment.
- **Silence after 'Any questions?'** → not always a bad sign. Many audiences, in Indonesia too, wait for someone else to go first (*sungkan*, *malu*). Give them a moment, then make it easier: *Here's a question I often get: …*, or *Turn to the person next to you for thirty seconds: what would you try first?*

**Running late:** never speed up to fit everything in, and never run over the next speaker's time. Cut, and say so calmly: *In the interest of time, I'll skip the third case study and go straight to what it means for you.* (*In the interests of time* is also common, especially in British English; both are fine.)

**When a joke falls flat** (*lelucon garing*): it happens to every speaker. Don't explain the joke, and don't apologise again and again. Smile, add one light line if you like (*OK, I'll leave comedy to the professionals.*), or simply move on. If you don't make it a big moment, the audience forgets it in ten seconds. **The Indonesian trap:** wordplay (*plesetan*) and jokes about local places rarely survive translation; with an international audience, humour from a short true story travels better.

id.text:
**Reading the room** (*membaca suasana*) berarti memperhatikan audiens selagi kamu bicara, dan mengubah pidatomu saat mereka memberi sinyal. Keynote adalah rencana, bukan naskah yang wajib diselesaikan kata per kata.

**Sinyal dan apa yang perlu dilakukan:**
- **Wajah bingung, orang berbisik ke sebelahnya** → mereka tertinggal. Ulangi dengan kata-kata sederhana dan contoh singkat: *Let me put that another way.* / *In other words, …*
- **Tatapan kosong saat ada istilah teknis** → lewati istilahnya (*jargon*) atau jelaskan dalam satu kalimat.
- **Ponsel mulai keluar, audiens gelisah, banyak yang bergeser di kursinya** → perhatian menurun, sering di bagian data yang panjang. Persingkat bagian itu, lompat ke cerita berikutnya, atau ajukan **pertanyaan angkat tangan** singkat: *Hands up if you've ever …*
- **Orang di belakang mencondongkan badan atau menaruh tangan di belakang telinga** → mereka tidak dengar. Bicara lebih keras, mendekat ke mikrofon, arahkan suara ke barisan paling belakang.
- **Mengernyit sambil menulis, 'Sorry, could you repeat that?'** → kamu terlalu cepat, sering saat menyebut angka. Pelankan tempo, ulangi angkanya, tampilkan di slide.
- **Tawa, anggukan, orang memotret slide** → pidatomu berhasil. Jangan buru-buru: biarkan tawa selesai, beri slide itu waktu sebentar.
- **Hening setelah 'Any questions?'** → belum tentu pertanda buruk. Banyak audiens, di Indonesia juga, menunggu orang lain bertanya duluan (*sungkan*, *malu*). Beri waktu sebentar, lalu permudah: *Here's a question I often get: …*, atau *Turn to the person next to you for thirty seconds: what would you try first?*

**Waktu hampir habis:** jangan pernah mempercepat bicara supaya semua masuk, dan jangan pernah memakai waktu pembicara berikutnya. Potong, dan katakan dengan tenang: *In the interest of time, I'll skip the third case study and go straight to what it means for you.* (*In the interests of time* juga umum, terutama dalam bahasa Inggris British; keduanya benar.)

**Saat lelucon garing:** ini terjadi pada setiap pembicara. Jangan jelaskan leluconnya, dan jangan minta maaf berulang-ulang. Tersenyumlah, tambahkan satu kalimat ringan kalau mau (*OK, I'll leave comedy to the professionals.*), atau langsung lanjutkan saja. Kalau kamu tidak membesar-besarkannya, audiens melupakannya dalam sepuluh detik. **Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** permainan kata (*plesetan*) dan lelucon tentang tempat-tempat lokal jarang berhasil saat diterjemahkan; untuk audiens internasional, humor dari cerita nyata yang singkat lebih mudah diterima.

blocks.text: **Plan your adaptations before you go on stage.** In your keyword notes, mark one section you can cut, one extra example for a hard point, and one show-of-hands question. Then reading the room becomes a choice, not a panic.

id.text: **Rencanakan penyesuaianmu sebelum naik panggung.** Di catatan kata kuncimu, tandai satu bagian yang bisa dipotong, satu contoh tambahan untuk poin yang sulit, dan satu pertanyaan angkat tangan. Dengan begitu, membaca suasana menjadi pilihan, bukan kepanikan.

blocks.prompt: Halfway through Budi's keynote in Jakarta, many people are looking at their phones during his long section of market data. What's the best move?
options: Speed up so that the data section ends sooner.
Stop and ask the audience to put their phones away.
Sum up the data in one sentence and move to his next customer story.
blocks.explain: Phones out during a long data section means attention is dropping, so **cut the section short** and go back to a story. Speeding up loses even the people still listening, and telling adults to put their phones away makes the room cold.

id.prompt: Di tengah keynote Budi di Jakarta, banyak orang melihat ponselnya saat dia membahas data pasar yang panjang. Apa langkah terbaik?
id.explain: Ponsel yang keluar di tengah bagian data yang panjang berarti perhatian menurun, jadi **persingkat bagian itu** dan kembali ke cerita. Bicara lebih cepat malah membuat orang yang masih mendengarkan ikut tertinggal, dan menyuruh orang dewasa menyimpan ponselnya membuat suasana jadi dingin.
options: Percepat bicara agar bagian data cepat selesai.
Berhenti dan minta audiens menyimpan ponsel.
Ringkas data dalam satu kalimat lalu lanjut ke cerita pelanggan berikutnya.

resources.title: TED's secret to great public speaking | Chris Anderson | TED
resources.note: A short talk by the head of TED: a great talk transfers one idea from the speaker's mind to the listeners', so limit it to one major idea and build it piece by piece. It matches this lesson's 'one big idea'. Natural native-speaker English: turn on the subtitles if you need them.

id.note: Pidato singkat dari pimpinan TED: pidato yang hebat memindahkan satu gagasan dari pikiran pembicara ke pikiran pendengar, jadi batasi pada satu gagasan utama dan bangun sedikit demi sedikit. Cocok dengan 'satu gagasan besar' di pelajaran ini. Bahasa Inggrisnya alami seperti penutur asli: nyalakan subtitle kalau perlu.

resources.title: How to Speak So That People Want to Listen | Julian Treasure | TED
resources.note: A sound expert on habits that make people stop listening and on the 'toolbox' of the voice: pace, pitch, volume and silence. Good for hearing real pauses and voice variety, which the app's single voice can't show. It also covers vocal warm-ups, beyond this lesson.

id.note: Seorang pakar suara membahas kebiasaan yang membuat orang berhenti mendengarkan dan 'kotak perkakas' suara: tempo, tinggi nada, volume dan keheningan. Bagus untuk mendengar jeda dan variasi suara yang nyata, yang tidak bisa ditunjukkan oleh satu suara di aplikasi. Video ini juga membahas pemanasan vokal, di luar cakupan pelajaran ini.

id.intro: Kamu sudah menulis teks persuasif dengan rule of three, anafora dan antitesis, dan suaramu sudah bisa membawa pujian, keraguan atau kehangatan. Sekarang semuanya kamu bawa ke atas panggung: pidato bergaya keynote yang dibangun di atas **satu gagasan besar**, retorika yang bekerja untuk telinga (jeda, pertanyaan, kontras, callback), dan keterampilan **membaca suasana** lalu menyesuaikan diri selagi kamu bicara. Pemanasan: ingat satu pidato yang masih kamu ingat sampai sekarang. Apa satu gagasan besarnya?
suggestedQuestions: Bagaimana cara menemukan satu gagasan besar kalau topik saya terasa terlalu luas?
Berapa lama sebaiknya saya diam setelah pertanyaan retoris?
Apa yang harus saya lakukan kalau waktu saya hampir habis di tengah pidato?
Bagaimana cara mempersingkat salam protokoler tanpa terkesan tidak sopan kepada para tamu VIP?

assessment.ps-1: Dalam pidato latihan bergaya TEDx di Bandung, Rina berkata: 'This city taught me to work hard. This city taught me to share. This city taught me never to give up.' Gaya bahasa apa itu? Pilih dari: antithesis, anaphora, rhetorical question, callback. Tulis namanya.
assessment.ps-2: Sari membuka keynote latihannya di sebuah startup summit di Jakarta dengan sebuah cerita: ponsel pertamanya layarnya retak, dan dia membuat aplikasi pertamanya di ponsel itu. Lima belas menit kemudian dia menutup: 'That cracked phone is still on my desk. Every morning, it reminds me who we build for.' Apa nama penutup yang kembali ke cerita pembuka? Pilih dari: hook, callback, signpost, preview. Tulis satu kata.
assessment.ps-3: Dimas menyampaikan pidato wisuda latihan di sebuah universitas di Yogyakarta. Dia mengajukan pertanyaan retoris kepada seisi aula: 'What would you do with one extra hour every day?' Apa yang sebaiknya dia lakukan tepat setelahnya? Pilih dari: answer it at once, pause, ask another question. Tulis pilihanmu dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.ps-4: Pak Hasan berbicara tanpa mikrofon di sebuah aula panjang di Surabaya. Dia melihat orang-orang di barisan belakang mencondongkan badan ke depan, dan seorang bapak menaruh tangan di belakang telinganya. Penyesuaian mana yang paling tepat? Pilih dari: speak louder, cut a section, tell a joke, skip the jargon. Tulis pilihanmu dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.ps-5: Pidato Rina di sebuah konferensi di Jakarta terlambat lima menit, dan pembicara berikutnya sudah menunggu. Dia ingin melewatkan studi kasus terakhirnya dengan tenang. Lengkapi dengan SATU kata: 'In the ___ of time, I'll skip the last case study and go straight to my conclusion.'
assessment.ps-6: Budi gugup dan menyebutkan angka-angka di keynote-nya di sebuah startup summit di Jakarta dengan sangat cepat. Beberapa orang mengernyit sambil berusaha mencatat angkanya, dan seseorang bertanya, 'Sorry, could you repeat that last number?' Penyesuaian mana yang paling tepat? Pilih dari: speed up, slow down, add a joke, skip the questions. Tulis pilihanmu dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.ps-7: Draf keynote latihan Dr. Wulan di Bandung berbunyi: 'Mistakes were made by our team.' Supaya enak didengar, dia mengubahnya menjadi kalimat aktif, sehingga pendengar tahu siapa melakukan apa. Lengkapi dengan SATU kata: 'Our team ___ mistakes.'
